sections.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
sections.narration: Welcome to the fascinating world of trigonometry! The word itself comes from Greek words 'trigonon', meaning triangle, and 'metron', meaning measure. At its core, trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that studies the relationships between the sides and angles of triangles. This might sound simple, but it's an incredibly powerful tool with applications everywhere, from building bridges and video games to astronomy and navigation. Imagine trying to find the height of a tall mountain without climbing it, or a ship trying to determine its distance from the shore. Trigonometry makes these seemingly impossible calculations possible. In this chapter, we will begin our journey by focusing on the fundamental building block of trigonometry: the right-angled triangle. We will learn about specific ratios of the sides of these triangles, called trigonometric ratios, which are the foundation for everything else that follows. Get ready to see triangles in a whole new light!

sections.title: Chapter Summary
sections.narration: In this chapter, we explored the fundamentals of trigonometry. We learned that trigonometry is the study of the relationship between the sides and angles of a right-angled triangle. We identified the three sides relative to an acute angle: the Hypotenuse (the longest side), the Opposite side (across from the angle), and the Adjacent side (next to the angle). We defined the six key trigonometric ratios: Sine (Opposite/Hypotenuse), Cosine (Adjacent/Hypotenuse), and Tangent (Opposite/Adjacent), often remembered by the mnemonic SOH CAH TOA. We also defined their reciprocal ratios: Cosecant (1/Sine), Secant (1/Cosine), and Cotangent (1/Tangent). Finally, we saw how the Pythagorean theorem, a² + b² = c², is essential for finding an unknown side length, allowing us to calculate all six trigonometric ratios even when only two sides are known.

sections.title: Trigonometric Ratios
sections.narration: To understand trigonometric ratios, we must first start with a special kind of triangle: the right-angled triangle. This is a triangle where one of the angles is exactly 90 degrees. The sides of this triangle have special names that are always defined relative to one of the other two angles, which we'll call angle 'A' for our example. The longest side, which is always opposite the right angle, is called the Hypotenuse. It's the 'sloped' side of the triangle. The side directly across from our angle A is called the Opposite side. And the remaining side, which is next to angle A but isn't the hypotenuse, is called the Adjacent side. 'Adjacent' just means 'next to'. These three names—Opposite, Adjacent, and Hypotenuse—are the building blocks for our ratios. There are six fundamental trigonometric ratios, which are simply specific fractions formed by the lengths of these three sides. The first three are Sine, Cosine, and Tangent. The sine of angle A, written as sin A, is the ratio of the length of the Opposite side to the length of the Hypotenuse. The cosine of angle A, or cos A, is the ratio of the Adjacent side to the Hypotenuse. And the tangent of angle A, or tan A, is the ratio of the Opposite side to the Adjacent side. We'll look at the other three ratios, their reciprocals, in a moment.

sections.title: Inverse of Trigonometric Ratios
sections.narration: Now that we've covered the three primary trigonometric ratios—Sine, Cosine, and Tangent—let's explore the other three. These are called the reciprocal ratios: Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent. The term 'reciprocal' is just a mathematical way of saying 'one divided by', or more simply, the 'flipped' version of a fraction. Each reciprocal ratio is paired with one of the primary ratios. Cosecant, written as csc A, is the reciprocal of sin A. So, if sin A is Opposite over Hypotenuse, then csc A is simply Hypotenuse over Opposite. We just flip the fraction. Next is Secant, written as sec A, which is the reciprocal of cos A. If cos A is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, then sec A becomes Hypotenuse over Adjacent. Again, we just flip the fraction. Finally, we have Cotangent, or cot A. This is the reciprocal of tan A. If tan A is Opposite over Adjacent, then cot A is Adjacent over Opposite. Understanding these reciprocal pairs is extremely helpful. It means you don't need to memorize six separate formulas. If you know SOH CAH TOA for Sine, Cosine, and Tangent, you can always find Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent just by flipping the fractions. This simple trick will be invaluable as you start solving trigonometric problems.

The term 'reciprocal' is just a mathematical way of saying 'one divided by', or more simply, the 'flipped' version of a fraction. Each reciprocal ratio is paired with one of the primary ratios.
Cosecant, written as csc A, is the reciprocal of sin A. So, if sin A is Opposite over Hypotenuse, then csc A is simply Hypotenuse over Opposite. We just flip the fraction.
Next is Secant, written as sec A, which is the reciprocal of cos A. If cos A is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, then sec A becomes Hypotenuse over Adjacent. Again, we just flip the fraction.
Finally, we have Cotangent, or cot A. This is the reciprocal of tan A. If tan A is Opposite over Adjacent, then cot A is Adjacent over Opposite.

Understanding these reciprocal pairs is extremely helpful. It means you don't need to memorize six separate formulas. If you know SOH CAH TOA for Sine, Cosine, and Tangent, you can always find Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent just by flipping the fractions. This simple trick will be invaluable as you start solving trigonometric problems.

sections.narration: Let's work through an example. Suppose we are given that for a certain angle A, tan A equals 4 over 3. Our goal is to find the other five trigonometric ratios. First, let's visualize this. We can draw a right-angled triangle ABC, with the right angle at B. Remember, tangent is the ratio of the Opposite side to the Adjacent side. Now we have two sides of our triangle, but we need the third side, the hypotenuse AC, to find the other ratios like sine and cosine. This is where the Pythagorean theorem comes in. It states that AC squared equals AB squared plus BC squared. Substituting our values, we get AC squared equals 3 squared plus 4 squared, which is 9 plus 16, giving us 25. Sin A is Opposite over Hypotenuse, which is 4 over 5. Cos A is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, which is 3 over 5. For the reciprocal ratios, we just flip the fractions: Csc A is the reciprocal of Sin A, so it's 5 over 4. Sec A is the reciprocal of Cos A, so it's 5 over 3. sections.title: Example 2: Prove ∠B = ∠Q from sin B = sin Q
sections.narration: This example is a bit more abstract and involves a proof. We are given two acute angles, B and Q, such that sin B is equal to sin Q. Our task is to prove that angle B must be equal to angle Q. Let's start by considering two separate right-angled triangles: triangle ABC, right-angled at C, and triangle PQR, right-angled at R. The given condition is sin B = sin Q. In triangle ABC, sin B is Opposite over Hypotenuse, which is AC over AB. In triangle PQR, sin Q is PR over PQ. So our equation is AC/AB = PR/PQ. Let's rearrange this slightly by swapping AB and PR. This gives us AC/PR = AB/PQ. This shows that the ratio of corresponding sides of the two triangles is constant. Let's call this constant 'k'. So, AC = k * PR and AB = k * PQ. Now, let's find the third side of each triangle using Pythagoras. For triangle ABC, the side BC is the square root of AB squared minus AC squared. For triangle PQR, the side QR is the square root of PQ squared minus PR squared. Let's substitute our 'k' expressions into the equation for BC. BC becomes the square root of (k*PQ) squared minus (k*PR) squared. We can factor out k-squared from under the root, which becomes k outside the root. This leaves us with BC = k times the square root of (PQ squared minus PR squared). Now look at the ratio of the third sides, BC over QR. It's k times the square root expression divided by the same square root expression. They cancel out, leaving us with BC/QR = k. This is amazing! We've now shown that AC/PR = AB/PQ = BC/QR. All three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio. By the Side-Side-Side (SSS) similarity criterion, this means that triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR. And if two triangles are similar, their corresponding angles must be equal. Therefore, angle B must be equal to angle Q, and our proof is complete.

sections.title: Example 3: Trigonometric Identity
sections.narration: Let's explore a very important trigonometric identity with this example. Consider a right-angled triangle ACB, where the right angle is at C. We're given that the hypotenuse AB is 29 units, and side BC is 21 units. The angle ABC is labeled as theta. Our task is to determine the values of two expressions: first, cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta, and second, cos-squared theta minus sin-squared theta. Before we can do anything, we need to find the length of the third side, AC. We use the Pythagorean theorem: AC equals the square root of AB squared minus BC squared. Plugging in the numbers, AC is the square root of 29 squared minus 21 squared. 29 squared is 841, and 21 squared is 441. The difference is 400. So, AC is the square root of 400, which is 20. Now we have all three sides: AC (Opposite to theta) is 20, BC (Adjacent to theta) is 21, and AB (Hypotenuse) is 29. Let's find sin theta and cos theta. Sin theta is Opposite over Hypotenuse, so it's 20 over 29. Cos theta is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, so it's 21 over 29. Now for the first part: cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta. This is (21/29) squared plus (20/29) squared. This equals 441 over 841 plus 400 over 841. Adding them together gives 841 over 841, which is exactly 1. This is a fundamental identity in trigonometry: for any angle theta, cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta is always 1. For the second part, cos-squared theta minus sin-squared theta. This is (21/29) squared minus (20/29) squared, which is 441 over 841 minus 400 over 841. The result is 41 over 841. This demonstrates how we can evaluate complex trigonometric expressions once we know the side lengths of the triangle.

segments.text: Let's explore a very important trigonometric identity with this example. Consider a right-angled triangle ACB, where the right angle is at C. We're given that the hypotenuse AB is 29 units, and side BC is 21 units. The angle ABC is labeled as theta.
Our task is to determine the values of two expressions: first, cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta, and second, cos-squared theta minus sin-squared theta.
Before we can do anything, we need to find the length of the third side, AC. We use the Pythagorean theorem: AC equals the square root of AB squared minus BC squared.
Plugging in the numbers, AC is the square root of 29 squared minus 21 squared. 29 squared is 841, and 21 squared is 441. The difference is 400. So, AC is the square root of 400, which is 20.
Now we have all three sides: AC (Opposite to theta) is 20, BC (Adjacent to theta) is 21, and AB (Hypotenuse) is 29.
Let's find sin theta and cos theta. Sin theta is Opposite over Hypotenuse, so it's 20 over 29. Cos theta is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, so it's 21 over 29.
Now for the first part: cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta. This is (21/29) squared plus (20/29) squared.
This equals 441 over 841 plus 400 over 841. Adding them together gives 841 over 841, which is exactly 1.
This is a fundamental identity in trigonometry: for any angle theta, cos-squared theta plus sin-squared theta is always 1.
For the second part, cos-squared theta minus sin-squared theta. This is (21/29) squared minus (20/29) squared, which is 441 over 841 minus 400 over 841. The result is 41 over 841.
This demonstrates how we can evaluate complex trigonometric expressions once we know the side lengths of the triangle.

From the given relationship, OQ - PQ = 1, we can express the hypotenuse OQ as 1 + PQ. This will be very useful.
Now, let's apply the Pythagorean theorem to triangle OPQ. The square of the hypotenuse, OQ squared, equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, OP squared plus PQ squared.
Now we can substitute what we know into this equation. We replace OQ with (1 + PQ) and OP with 7. The equation becomes (1 + PQ) squared equals 7 squared plus PQ squared.
Let's expand the left side: 1 squared is 1, 2 times 1 times PQ is 2PQ, and PQ squared is PQ squared. So we have 1 + 2PQ + PQ squared equals 49 + PQ squared.
Notice that PQ squared appears on both sides of the equation, so we can cancel them out. This simplifies things greatly, leaving us with 1 + 2PQ = 49.
Now we can solve for PQ. Subtracting 1 from both sides gives 2PQ = 48. Dividing by 2, we find that PQ = 24 cm.
Now that we have PQ, we can easily find OQ using our earlier relationship: OQ = 1 + PQ, which is 1 + 24, so OQ = 25 cm.
We have all three sides: OP = 7, PQ = 24, and OQ = 25. Finally, we can find sin Q and cos Q.

For angle Q, the opposite side is OP and the adjacent side is PQ. So, sin Q, which is Opposite over Hypotenuse, is OP/OQ or 7 over 25. And cos Q, which is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, is PQ/OQ or 24 over 25.

flashcards.title: The Chief's Secret Code
flashcards.explanation: The most famous mnemonic of all! It stands for: Sine = Opposite / Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent / Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite / Adjacent. Just chant 'SOH CAH TOA' to remember the three primary ratios.

flashcards.title: Flipping Friends
flashcards.mnemonic: Cosecant flips Sine, Secant flips Cosine, Cotangent flips Tangent.
flashcards.explanation: To get the reciprocal ratios, just find their 'flipping friend' and turn the fraction upside down. Cosecant (csc) is the flip of Sine (sin), Secant (sec) is the flip of Cosine (cos), and Cotangent (cot) is the flip of Tangent (tan).

flashcards.title: Pythagoras's Square Dance
flashcards.mnemonic: Two small squares dance to make one big one.
flashcards.explanation: Remember that the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides (legs) is equal to the square of the longest side (hypotenuse). In a triangle with sides a, b and hypotenuse c: a² + b² = c². This is your key to finding a missing side.

recap_scenes.description: The foundation of trigonometry is the right-angled triangle. Its sides have special names relative to an angle.
recap_scenes.wan_prompt: Flat vector illustration, bright colors, Indian educational textbook style, purple and blue gradient background. A friendly cartoon architect character stands next to a large glowing blueprint of a right-angled triangle. As the architect points, the sides light up one by one with labels: 'Hypotenuse' (the longest, sloped side), 'Opposite' (the side across from the angle), and 'Adjacent' (the side next to the angle). An eye icon sits at the angle to show the perspective.
recap_scenes.narration: Everything in basic trigonometry begins with the right-angled triangle. It's our stage. For any chosen angle, which we call theta, the sides get special names. The longest side, always opposite the 90-degree corner, is the Hypotenuse. The side directly across from our angle theta is the Opposite. And the side right next to theta, that isn't the hypotenuse, is the Adjacent. Mastering these three names is the first crucial step to understanding all the ratios.

recap_scenes.concept_title: The Magic Words: SOH CAH TOA
recap_scenes.description: The mnemonic SOH CAH TOA is the key to remembering the three main trigonometric ratios.
recap_scenes.wan_prompt: Flat vector illustration, bright colors, Indian educational textbook style, purple and blue gradient background. A student in a blue school uniform sits at a desk, looking puzzled at a triangle. A wise old owl character appears and whispers 'SOH CAH TOA'. As the student repeats the words, three glowing formulas animate out of a book: Sinθ=Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosθ=Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tanθ=Opposite/Adjacent. The student's face lights up with understanding.
recap_scenes.narration: How do we remember the formulas for the main ratios? With a simple, powerful mnemonic: SOH CAH TOA. It's like a secret code. SOH tells us that Sine equals Opposite divided by Hypotenuse. CAH reminds us that Cosine equals Adjacent divided by Hypotenuse. And TOA shows that Tangent equals Opposite divided by Adjacent. By just remembering these three short words, you hold the key to the three most important functions in trigonometry. It's the most valuable phrase you'll learn.

recap_scenes.description: Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent are the 'flipped' versions of Sine, Cosine, and Tangent.
recap_scenes.wan_prompt: Flat vector illustration, bright colors, Indian educational textbook style, purple and blue gradient background. Three primary ratios (Sin, Cos, Tan) are shown as solid blocks. With a flipping animation, they turn over to reveal their reciprocals (Csc, Sec, Cot) on the other side. For example, the 'Sin' block with the fraction 'O/H' flips over to become a 'Csc' block with the fraction 'H/O'. Arrows connect the pairs to show the relationship.
recap_scenes.narration: Beyond the main three, there are three more ratios called reciprocal ratios: Cosecant, Secant, and Cotangent. The best way to think of them is as 'flipping friends'. Cosecant is just the sine ratio flipped upside down. Secant is the cosine ratio flipped over. And Cotangent is the tangent ratio flipped. You don't need to memorize six different formulas from scratch; if you know SOH CAH TOA, you automatically know the other three just by inverting the fractions. They always come in these pairs.

recap_scenes.description: The Pythagorean theorem, a² + b² = c², is used to find a missing side of a right triangle.
recap_scenes.wan_prompt: Flat vector illustration, bright colors, Indian educational textbook style, purple and blue gradient background. A right-angled triangle has two sides labeled '3' and '4'. A question mark is on the hypotenuse. A magical animation shows a 3x3 square and a 4x4 square of blocks. The blocks then flow and reassemble into a single 5x5 square on the hypotenuse, revealing the missing side length is '5'. The formula a²+b²=c² glows brightly.
recap_scenes.narration: What happens if you only know two sides of a right-angled triangle? You can always find the third using the ancient and powerful Pythagorean theorem. It states that if you square the lengths of the two shorter sides, 'a' and 'b', their sum will equal the square of the hypotenuse, 'c'. This formula, a-squared plus b-squared equals c-squared, is your ultimate tool for filling in the blanks. It’s essential for solving almost any trigonometry problem where a side is missing.

recap_scenes.description: By combining ratios and Pythagoras, we can solve for any unknown side or angle.
recap_scenes.wan_prompt: Flat vector illustration, bright colors, Indian educational textbook style, purple and blue gradient background. A student in a blue school uniform stands before a large toolkit labeled 'Trigonometry'. The tools are 'SOH CAH TOA' (a wrench), 'Pythagoras' (a hammer), and 'Reciprocals' (a screwdriver). The student confidently picks a tool and applies it to a triangle with missing parts, which then fill in with glowing numbers. The student gives a thumbs-up.
recap_scenes.narration: The real power of trigonometry comes when you combine these tools. If you're given a right triangle with some information—like one side and one angle, or two sides—you can solve for everything else. First, see if you can use SOH CAH TOA. If you're missing a side needed for the ratio, use Pythagoras to find it first. By switching between the trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean theorem, no right-angled triangle can hide its secrets from you. You have a complete toolkit to solve them all.
